incidents.title: One tenant dominates a shard
incidents.brief: A single tenant creates 70% of all writes, but the data is stored in one shard.
incidents.constraint: The hottest user still produces a hotspot.
incidents.question: What is the correct fix?

choices.label: Re-shard on (tenant_id, hash(user_id)) to split the whale
choices.resultBody: Compound partition keys distribute the whale tenant's high write volume across multiple physical database instances, eliminating the single-shard hotspot.

choices.label: Put an in-memory cache in front of the whale tenant's queries
choices.resultBody: Caches absorb read traffic, but 80% of this tenant's traffic consists of write operations that must hit persistent disk, leaving the database shard at 98% CPU.

choices.label: Upgrade the shard to the largest instance size at $4,500/mo
choices.resultBody: The $4,500/mo instance drops CPU for a few weeks, but the whale tenant still sends 70% of writes to one node, and its growth saturates the new box within 6 weeks.

hints: One partition is a hotspot.
Key choice drives skew.
Spread the hot key.

incidents.title: One flash-sale counter pins shard 5
incidents.brief: A sneaker drop sends 40,000 'units sold' increments/s to a single row. Hash sharding put that row on shard 5, now at 96% CPU with lock waits; the other 11 shards idle below 20%.
incidents.constraint: The counter must stay exact, and the product page reads it once per second.
incidents.question: How do you spread the writes for this one key?

choices.label: Split the counter into 32 salted sub-keys summed on read
choices.resultBody: Each increment picks counter:sku-991:{0..31} at random, so the 32 sub-rows hash to different shards and no single row lock serialises 40,000 writes. The page's once-a-second read sums 32 rows, which is cheap.

choices.label: Add two read replicas to shard 5 to absorb the increment load
choices.resultBody: Every increment is a write, and writes still go to shard 5's primary; the replicas just replay the same 40,000 updates/s and lag behind.

choices.label: Move shard 5 to an instance with twice the CPU cores and RAM
choices.resultTitle: One row lock, more idle cores
choices.resultBody: All increments contend for the same row lock, so they run one at a time no matter how many cores the box has; latency barely moves.

hints: The problem is one key, not the shard layout.
A single row can only take one write at a time.
Turn one hot key into many keys and add them up on read.

incidents.title: Team wants to shard a 200 GB table
incidents.brief: The users table is 200 GB with 3,000 writes/s, and the primary sits at 94% CPU. Engineers propose sharding to 8 nodes. The slow-query log shows 80% of CPU in one lookup by (org_id, email) doing a sequential scan.
incidents.constraint: A sharding project would take the team a full quarter.
incidents.question: What should happen first?

choices.label: Add a composite index on (org_id, email) and hold off on sharding
choices.resultBody: The lookup becomes an index seek, CPU falls from 94% to about 22%, and one node handles 3,000 writes/s with years of headroom. Sharding would have spread the same bad query across 8 nodes.

choices.label: Shard the users table by hash(user_id) across 8 nodes right away
choices.resultTitle: Eight nodes scanning instead of one
choices.resultBody: The lookup filters by org_id and email, not user_id, so every call now fans out to all 8 shards and each still runs the sequential scan.

choices.label: Add a read replica and route the email lookup query to it
choices.resultTitle: Replica pinned by the same scan
choices.resultBody: The replica runs the same unindexed scan and hits 95% CPU within minutes, while the primary still pays for the scans inside write transactions.

hints: What is actually using the CPU?
200 GB and 3,000 writes/s fit on one modern node.
Fix the access path before splitting the data.

incidents.title: Order history page fans out to 16 shards
incidents.brief: BazaarGo shards orders by hash(order_id) over 16 Postgres shards. The 'My orders' page, 70% of order reads, needs all of one user's orders, so each of 20k views/s queries all 16 shards; p95 is 1.4 s.
incidents.constraint: Single-order lookups by order_id must stay a one-shard read.
incidents.question: How do you make a user's order history a one-shard query?

choices.label: Reshard orders by hash(user_id); embed shard in order_id
choices.resultBody: All of a user's orders now live together, so history is one indexed query on one shard and p95 drops to 45 ms. Encoding the shard number in each new order_id keeps lookups by order_id single-shard too. Cost: a backfill migration, and very heavy buyers can make their shard a bit hotter.

choices.label: Run the 16 shard queries in parallel with a 300 ms timeout
choices.resultBody: Latency is capped at 420 ms, but every view still costs 16 queries, CPU stays at 85%, and whenever one shard is slow the page silently drops that shard's orders.

choices.label: Cache each user's full order history in Redis for an hour
choices.resultBody: Repeat views are fast, but a user who just ordered sees the old list for up to an hour, and every cache miss still fans out to 16 shards, so CPU only falls to 70%.

hints: Which query is the hot path, and which column does it filter on?
Data read together should be stored together.
The shard key should match the page's main filter, while still letting you find one order.

incidents.title: One shard down, whole app down
incidents.brief: Shard 9 of 24 loses its primary during failover. Only 4% of tenants live there, yet 100% of requests fail, because every request first loads feature flags from a table that lives only on shard 9.
incidents.constraint: Shard 9 needs about 10 minutes to promote a replica.
incidents.question: How do you stop one shard from taking everyone down?

choices.label: Cache flags in each app node and fail only shard 9's tenants
choices.resultBody: Flags come from a local copy refreshed every 30 s, so requests no longer touch shard 9 unless the tenant lives there. 96% of tenants recover at once; shard 9's tenants get a clear error until promotion finishes.

choices.label: Restart the whole app fleet to clear stuck database connections
choices.resultTitle: Fresh pods hit the same dead shard
choices.resultBody: New pods start, try to load flags from shard 9, and block on the same timeout; the restart adds a cold-start wave on top of the outage.

choices.label: Raise every shard query timeout from 5 seconds to 30 seconds
choices.resultBody: Promotion takes 10 minutes, so a 30 s wait still ends in failure, and every request now ties up a worker six times longer.

hints: Only 4% of tenants live on shard 9. Why is everyone failing?
Something every request needs lives on one shard.
Keep global data off a single shard and scope failures to their tenants.

incidents.title: The 'card' shard takes 85% of all orders
incidents.brief: PayNest shards 9,000 order writes/s by payment_method: card, wallet, bank, cash. Cards are 85% of orders, so shard 'card' runs at 97% CPU while the other three idle below 15%.
incidents.constraint: Adding hardware to the card shard is capped: it is already the largest instance type.
incidents.question: What shard key spreads the writes evenly?

choices.label: Reshard by hash(customer_id) across 16 shards
choices.resultBody: customer_id has millions of values, so hashing it gives every shard about 1/16 of the writes at ~42% CPU and keeps each customer's orders together. Cost: 'all card orders' reports now scatter across shards, and the migration needs a backfill.

choices.label: Split the card shard into Visa and Mastercard shards
choices.resultTitle: The Visa shard is the new hotspot
choices.resultBody: Visa is 70% of card volume, so the new Visa shard runs at 78% CPU. The key still has only a handful of values, so the next growth spurt or card network promo overloads it again.

choices.label: Add three read replicas to the card shard
choices.resultBody: The load is 9,000 writes/s, and every replica must replay them all. The primary stays at 96% CPU and replicas start lagging behind it.

hints: Count how many distinct values the shard key has.
A key with four values can never use more than four shards evenly, and only if they are equally common.
Pick a key with high cardinality that spreads writes uniformly.

incidents.title: A celebrity's profile pins one shard at 95%
incidents.brief: Chirp shards profiles by hash(user_id) over 32 shards. A pop star with 90M followers posts, and her profile row takes 180k reads/s. Shard 14 hits 95% CPU; every other user on it times out.
incidents.constraint: Profile edits must show up within 10 seconds; the other 31 shards are near 30%.
incidents.question: How do you absorb 180k reads/s on a single row?

choices.label: Cache hot profiles in Redis and app memory for 5 seconds
choices.resultTitle: The row is read once per 5 seconds
choices.resultBody: Each API node holds the profile in memory for 5 s, backed by Redis, so shard 14 sees a handful of reads per second for that row and returns to 32% CPU. Edits appear within 5 s, inside the 10 s budget. Cost: another layer to invalidate and a brief window of stale profiles.

choices.label: Reshard from 32 to 64 shards to spread the celebrity's load
choices.resultTitle: One row still lives on one shard
choices.resultBody: The week-long reshard halves everyone else's load, but a single user_id always hashes to exactly one shard. That shard still receives all 180k reads/s and stays at 94% CPU.

choices.label: Move the celebrity to her own largest-size instance
choices.resultBody: Other users on shard 14 recover, but one database node still has to serve 180k reads/s of the same row and runs at 88% CPU. The next viral account needs its own machine too.

hints: The load is on one row, not one range of rows.
No sharding scheme can split a single key across machines.
The data barely changes; how many of those reads need to reach the database?

incidents.title: One merchant's partition lags 40 minutes
incidents.brief: ShopRail's order-events topic has 24 partitions keyed by merchant_id. A flash sale gives one merchant 60% of 50k events/s, so partition 7 lags 40 minutes while the other 23 consumers sit idle.
incidents.constraint: Consumers need ordering only per order_id (created, paid, shipped), not per merchant.
incidents.question: How do you spread one merchant's events across consumers?

choices.label: Key events by order_id instead of merchant_id
choices.resultTitle: The flash sale spreads over 24 partitions
choices.resultBody: Each order's events still land on one partition in order, but the merchant's thousands of orders hash across all 24, so every consumer takes a share at ~45% CPU and lag drains in minutes. Cost: per-merchant aggregations must now combine data from all partitions.

choices.label: Grow the topic from 24 to 96 partitions
choices.resultBody: The merchant_id still hashes to exactly one partition, now one of 96. That partition and its single consumer keep 60% of the traffic, and adding partitions also reshuffles key placement for everyone else.

choices.label: Scale the consumer group from 24 to 72 instances
choices.resultBody: A partition is read by at most one consumer in a group, so the 48 new instances get no partitions assigned. Partition 7's consumer is still the bottleneck.

hints: A partition is consumed by only one consumer in a group.
The partition key decides which events share a partition.
Choose the narrowest key that still preserves the ordering you actually need.

incidents.title: Enterprise tenant fills shard 3's disk to 92%
incidents.brief: LedgerLoop routes tenants to 12 shards via a directory. Acme Corp grew from 200 GB to 3.1 TB this year; shard 3's 4 TB disk is 92% full, growing 60 GB weekly, and its 70 other tenants slow down.
incidents.constraint: Contracts require 7 years of history online; Acme's queries all filter by its tenant_id.
incidents.question: Where should Acme's data live?

choices.label: Move Acme to its own shard, then flip its directory entry
choices.resultTitle: Acme gets a home of its own
choices.resultBody: Acme's rows are copied to a new shard with live replication, and one directory update switches its routing, so shard 3 drops to 18% disk and its 70 neighbours stop suffering. Cost: one more shard to run, and Acme's shard must be sized and scaled on its own.

choices.label: Split shard 3 into two shards by hash(tenant_id)
choices.resultTitle: Acme lands on one half, intact
choices.resultBody: Hashing tenant_id moves whole tenants, so all 3.1 TB of Acme ends up on one of the halves. That half is at 80% disk and fills again in about ten weeks.

choices.label: Archive Acme's data older than 90 days to cold storage
choices.resultBody: Disk drops to 40%, but auditors and Acme's finance team can no longer query history older than 90 days, which the contract requires to stay online for 7 years.

hints: The issue is one tenant's size, not the total number of tenants.
Any hash of tenant_id keeps a tenant's rows together.
A directory lets you place a single tenant anywhere you like.

incidents.title: North America shard melts, APAC idles
incidents.brief: TripNest partitions bookings by region. North America produces 62% of 9k writes/s, so the NA shard sits at 95% CPU with 2.1 s p95 while EU and APAC idle near 20%.
incidents.constraint: Bookings must stay in their legal region and remain queryable by region for reporting.
incidents.question: How do you spread NA load without breaking residency?

choices.label: Sub-shard NA by (region, hash(booking_id) mod 4)
choices.resultBody: NA bookings spread over four NA sub-shards at ~45% CPU each and p95 falls from 2,100 to 140 ms, with every row still in-region. Cost: "all NA bookings" reports scatter-gather across 4 shards, and the move needs a dual-write migration.

choices.label: Spill NA overflow writes onto the idle APAC shard
choices.resultBody: NA CPU drops to 80%, but spilled bookings cross a 150 ms Pacific round trip, US customer data now sits in APAC (legal flags it within the hour), and NA reports miss 20% of rows.

choices.label: Upgrade the NA shard to a 3x larger instance
choices.resultBody: CPU falls to 62% and p95 to 480 ms, but NA still carries 62% of writes on one node at triple the price, and the summer booking peak will saturate it again.

hints: Region is a fine locality key but a terrible balance key.
The fix must keep NA rows in NA and still split NA traffic.
Add a second, well-distributed component under the region prefix.

incidents.title: Two customers received the same order number
incidents.brief: After splitting orders across 8 MySQL shards, each shard kept its own AUTO_INCREMENT. Order #48213377 now exists on shards 2 and 5; 1,400 support tickets and duplicate invoices in 3 days.
incidents.constraint: IDs must stay 64-bit integers and roughly time-ordered, because the mobile app paginates by id.
incidents.question: How do you generate unique ids across shards?

choices.label: Snowflake-style ids: timestamp, shard number, sequence
choices.resultBody: Each id packs 41 bits of milliseconds, 10 bits of shard or worker number and a 12-bit sequence, so no two shards can ever mint the same value, ids stay 64-bit and time-sortable, and no network call is needed. Cost: clocks must be monitored, since a clock stepping backwards can repeat ids unless the generator waits.

choices.label: Issue every id from one central AUTO_INCREMENT table
choices.resultTitle: A new single point of failure
choices.resultBody: Duplicates stop, but all 30,000 inserts/s now wait on one database for an id. It runs at 96% CPU, adds a network hop to every insert, and when it fails every shard stops taking orders.

choices.label: Switch every primary key to a random UUIDv4 value
choices.resultBody: Random 128-bit ids are unique, but they are not 64-bit and not time-ordered, so the app's pagination by id breaks, and random inserts scatter across the B-tree, raising insert latency to 95 ms.

hints: Each shard is counting on its own, starting from the same place.
Uniqueness can come from coordination, or from structure inside the id itself.
What if part of every id identified the shard that created it?

incidents.title: Currency joins turn every invoice into 2 queries
incidents.brief: InvoiceHub shards invoices by customer across 24 shards, but the 40 MB currencies and tax_rates tables live in one central database. Every invoice render does a remote lookup; 45k lookups/s pin it at 94% CPU.
incidents.constraint: Tax rates change a few times a month and must take effect everywhere within a minute.
incidents.question: Where should the small reference tables live?

choices.label: Replicate the reference tables to every shard
choices.resultBody: Each shard holds a read-only copy of the 40 MB tables, kept current by logical replication within seconds, so invoice queries join locally and the central DB only takes the rare writes. p95 drops to 35 ms. Cost: 24 copies to monitor, and a rate change applies shard by shard over a few seconds.

choices.label: Shard currencies and tax rates by code as well
choices.resultBody: A tiny table does not need sharding. Each invoice's customer shard rarely holds its currency or tax row, so a single render now touches two or three shards and p95 climbs to 520 ms.

choices.label: Add four read replicas to the central reference DB
choices.resultBody: CPU per node falls to 45%, but every invoice still makes an extra network round trip per lookup, often several per invoice, so p95 only improves to 260 ms and you run five databases for 40 MB of data.

hints: How big are the tables everyone joins against?
Not every table in a sharded system has to be sharded.
Small, rarely changing data can be copied rather than partitioned.

incidents.title: Resharding plan needs an 11-hour write freeze
incidents.brief: MealMate must split 4 shards into 16 to handle growth. The plan is dump-and-restore of 8 TB, which needs an 11-hour write freeze. The shards are at 88% CPU and orders never stop.
incidents.constraint: Checkout can tolerate at most a few seconds of write pause, per shard range.
incidents.question: How do you move 8 TB without stopping writes?

choices.label: Backfill new shards, stream changes via CDC, cut over per range
choices.resultBody: A snapshot backfills the 16 new shards while change-data-capture replays every write since the snapshot. When lag is near zero, each range pauses writes for a few seconds, flips its routing entry and resumes. Cost: weeks of tooling, verification checksums, and double storage during the move.

choices.label: Copy a snapshot to all 16 new shards, then flip the router
choices.resultBody: The copy takes 11 hours, and nothing carries over the writes made during those hours. After the switch, about 3,200 orders placed mid-copy exist only on the old shards.

choices.label: Dual-write to old and new shards, then switch reads over
choices.resultTitle: New rows present, old rows missing
choices.resultBody: Writes from now on reach both sides, but the 8 TB of existing rows were never backfilled, so reads switched to the new shards miss every order older than the dual-write start. Partial failures between the two writes also let the copies diverge.

hints: Copying takes hours; the question is what happens to writes during those hours.
You need both the existing data and a record of every change made since.
Catch up continuously, then switch each range once it is nearly in sync.

incidents.title: Newest shard range takes every insert
incidents.brief: EventPipe range-shards events on a time-ordered UUIDv1-style id. All 40k inserts/s land in the newest range, pinning shard 8 at 97% CPU while shards 1-7 idle at 10%.
incidents.constraint: Consumers fetch events by id only; ordering lives in a separate timestamp column.
incidents.question: What key property removes the hot tail range?

choices.label: Route by hash of the event id across all 8 shards
choices.resultBody: Hashing spreads 40k inserts/s at ~5k per shard; the hottest shard falls from 97% to 38% CPU and p95 from 1,800 to 35 ms. Cost: id-ordered range scans now hit all 8 shards, and existing rows need a backfill.

choices.label: Split the hot range more often with auto-splitting
choices.resultTitle: The hot spot follows the tail
choices.resultBody: The splitter keeps carving the tail range, but new ids are always the largest, so every insert goes to whichever split is newest. Shard CPU stays at 96%.

choices.label: Switch the keys to auto-increment integers on each shard
choices.resultBody: Auto-increment keys are just as monotonic as time-ordered UUIDs: inserts still target the top of the key space, and the id allocator adds a coordination hop, so p95 reaches 2,000 ms.

hints: The ids look random, but they always increase.
Range sharding on an increasing key always has one hot end.
Make shard placement independent of when the row was created.

incidents.title: Monthly admin report slows every tenant
incidents.brief: CRMly's finance report sums revenue over 18 months across all 40 tenant shards. Each run scans 6 TB, takes 3 hours and pushes shards to 92% CPU; tenant dashboards hit 4 s p95 while it runs.
incidents.constraint: Finance wants the report daily now, and customers span every time zone.
incidents.question: Where should cross-tenant analytics run?

choices.label: Stream shard changes via CDC into a columnar warehouse
choices.resultBody: Change-data-capture tails each shard's log into a columnar warehouse, so the report scans compressed columns in minutes and never touches the shards, which return to 38% CPU. Cost: warehouse spend, a pipeline to operate, and data that is a few minutes behind.

choices.label: Run the scatter-gather report nightly at 2 a.m. UTC
choices.resultBody: With tenants in every time zone there is no quiet hour. The 3-hour scan now slows APAC dashboards every single day instead of once a month.

choices.label: Point the report at one read replica per shard
choices.resultBody: Dashboards recover, but you now run 40 extra databases, each still scanning row-oriented tables for 3 hours, and replicas lag during the scan, so failover safety suffers.

hints: The workload that hurts is rare, huge and read-only.
Transactional shards are tuned for small, indexed queries per tenant.
Give the analytics a copy of the data in a store built for scans.

incidents.title: Two hottest shards share one host
incidents.brief: GameHive runs 64 logical shards on 16 hosts. After a rebalance by disk size, shards 9 and 41, the busiest (league and tournament data), landed on host H3: 96% CPU while hosts average 40%.
incidents.constraint: The shard key and shard count are fine; a full reshard would take weeks.
incidents.question: What is the quickest correct fix for host H3?

choices.label: Move shard 41 to idle host H7 and balance by load
choices.resultBody: A replica of shard 41 is built on H7, promoted, and the routing map updated, so H3 drops to 55% and H7 rises to 60%. The balancer now weighs CPU and QPS, not just disk. Cost: one shard's data copied across the network, throttled to protect live traffic.

choices.label: Reshard all 64 shards onto a new league-based key
choices.resultTitle: Weeks of work for a placement bug
choices.resultBody: The key was never the problem: the load is simply stacked on one host. The reshard project starts, and H3 stays at 96% for the weeks it takes.

choices.label: Upgrade host H3 to an instance with twice the cores
choices.resultBody: H3 recovers to 62%, but it now costs twice as much while H7 idles at 22%, and the disk-only balancer can stack hot shards together again at the next rebalance.

hints: Compare load per host, not per shard.
Logical shards can move between hosts without changing any keys.
Balance on the resource that is actually saturated.

incidents.title: Money vanishes between two wallet shards
incidents.brief: CoinPocket shards wallets by user_id over 12 shards. A transfer debits the sender's shard, then credits the receiver's. When the app crashes between the two writes, money disappears: $18k across 240 transfers last week.
incidents.constraint: Transfers may show 'pending' for a few seconds, but shard primaries must not hold locks across network calls.
incidents.question: How do you make a cross-shard transfer never lose money?

choices.label: Commit the debit with an outbox row; apply credits idempotently
choices.resultTitle: Every debit carries its own receipt
choices.resultBody: The debit and a 'credit pending' outbox row commit in one local transaction on the sender's shard. A relay delivers it to the receiver's shard, which applies the credit keyed by transfer_id, so crashes cause a retry, never a loss or a double credit. Cost: transfers are eventually consistent for a second or two.

choices.label: Wrap debit and credit in a two-phase commit across shards
choices.resultTitle: Atomic, but locks wait on the network
choices.resultBody: Losses stop, but both shards now hold row locks through the prepare and commit round trips. Hot wallets queue behind each other, p95 rises to 420 ms, and a coordinator crash leaves transactions in doubt, holding locks until someone resolves them.

choices.label: Retry the credit from the app with backoff until it succeeds
choices.resultTitle: The retry dies with the process
choices.resultBody: Retries help with network blips, but the pending credit lives only in memory. When the pod crashes or is redeployed between the two writes, nothing remembers the transfer, and money still disappears.

hints: A crash can happen at any instant between the two writes.
Something durable must record the obligation in the same commit as the debit.
Record the intent locally, then deliver it until the other side confirms, safely repeatable.

incidents.title: Adding a fifth shard would move 80% of rows
incidents.brief: QuizUp routes users with user_id % 4. The four shards hold 6 TB and run at 86% CPU. Switching to % 5 remaps about 80% of keys, roughly 4.8 TB of copying before shard 5 helps.
incidents.constraint: Future growth will add shards every few months, and each move must be small and throttled.
incidents.question: How should keys map to shards so growth moves little data?

choices.label: Hash keys into 1,024 fixed slots; move whole slots
choices.resultTitle: Only the new shard's share moves
choices.resultBody: Keys hash to 1,024 slots and a small table maps slots to shards. Adding shard 4 reassigns about 205 slots, moving only the 20% of data it should own, slot by slot and throttled, with no other key changing place. Cost: every router must fetch and cache the slot table.

choices.label: Switch routing to user_id % 5 over one weekend
choices.resultTitle: 4.8 TB on the move at once
choices.resultBody: Four of every five users change shard, so the weekend is spent copying 4.8 TB while the old shards run at 99% CPU. Reads for rows not yet copied miss, and the next shard will require the same ordeal.

choices.label: Route only new signups to a fifth shard and leave the rest
choices.resultTitle: Old shards keep all the load
choices.resultBody: No data moves, but the existing users generating 95% of traffic stay on shards 0-3 at 84% CPU, and shard 4 fills only with new signups, which are the most active cohort for a few weeks and then idle.

hints: With modulo, changing N changes the answer for most keys.
Add a layer of indirection between the hash and the physical shard.
Fix the number of buckets once, and move buckets instead of rehashing keys.

incidents.title: Leaderboard page 200 takes 9 seconds
incidents.brief: ArenaX shards 20M players by player_id over 16 shards. The global leaderboard fetches the top page x 50 rows from every shard and merges, so page 200 reads 160,000 rows; shards hit 90% CPU.
incidents.constraint: Scores update 25,000 times per second and ranks may be at most a few seconds behind.
incidents.question: How do you serve a global ranking over sharded data?

choices.label: Keep the ranking in a Redis sorted set fed by score events
choices.resultTitle: Any page in one O(log n) call
choices.resultBody: Each score change publishes an event that does ZADD on a single sorted set of 20M members, about 2 GB of RAM. Any page is one ZREVRANGE call returning 50 rows in milliseconds, and shards stop doing ranking work. Cost: a derived store to rebuild from the shards if Redis is lost.

choices.label: Merge only the top 50 rows from each shard for every page
choices.resultBody: The merge now reads 800 rows and returns quickly, but page 2 onward can only be correct if every shard contributes enough rows. Players on one shard vanish from pages where they belong, and rank numbers disagree with profiles.

choices.label: Move every score into one unsharded scores table with an index
choices.resultBody: Ranking queries use a single index now, but all 25,000 score updates per second land on one database, which saturates at 97% CPU. The reason for sharding comes straight back.

hints: A global order needs a structure that sees every player at once.
Deep offsets across N shards cost N times the offset.
Keep the rank in a structure built for ordered insert and range lookup.

incidents.title: Writes keep landing on the shard a row left
incidents.brief: HomeStay moved 3% of listings from shard 3 to shard 7 last night. API nodes cache the shard directory for 10 minutes, so for each move they kept writing to shard 3; 1,900 bookings went to the old location.
incidents.constraint: The directory service handles about 50 req/s; there are 400 API nodes.
incidents.question: How do routers learn about a move before they cause damage?

choices.label: Shards reject stale map versions; routers refresh and retry
choices.resultTitle: Wrong shard says 'moved', router fixes itself
choices.resultBody: Every request carries the router's map version. Shard 3 knows it no longer owns the range and replies MOVED with the new owner, so the router refreshes its map and retries on shard 7. Misroutes are rejected instead of written, and directory load stays near 50 req/s. Cost: one extra round trip per router after each move.

choices.label: Cut the routers' directory cache TTL to 5 seconds
choices.resultBody: 400 nodes refreshing every 5 seconds turn 50 req/s into thousands, pushing the directory to 95% CPU. There is still a 5-second window where writes land on shard 3 after each move.

choices.label: Have shard 3 relay writes for moved rows through to shard 7
choices.resultTitle: The old shard becomes a relay
choices.resultBody: Bookings reach shard 7, but shard 3 now proxies every write for rows it gave away, so its CPU rises to 70% and p95 doubles. After a second move, requests chain through multiple forwarding hops.

hints: The directory is correct; the routers' copies are the problem.
Only the shard knows for sure which ranges it currently owns.
Let the wrong destination refuse the request and point to the right one.

incidents.title: Email login fans out to 32 shards
incidents.brief: Accounts are sharded by user_id across 32 Postgres shards. Login looks users up by email, so each of 12k logins/s queries all 32 shards and waits for the slowest one.
incidents.constraint: user_id stays the shard key; profiles and orders are co-located with it.
incidents.question: How does login find the right shard?

choices.label: Email-to-user_id lookup table, sharded by email hash
choices.resultBody: Login reads the email's lookup shard, then the one user shard: 2 point reads instead of 32. Shard CPU falls from 88% to 24% and p95 to 18 ms. Cost: signup and email changes must write both records, via an outbox so they never drift.

choices.label: Add a secondary index on email to each of the 32 shards
choices.resultBody: Each shard answers in 2 ms instead of scanning, so CPU drops to 70%, but every login still sends 32 queries and waits for the slowest shard; p95 only improves to 410 ms.

choices.label: Cache email-to-shard lookups in Redis keyed by email
choices.resultTitle: Logins are too rare to cache
choices.resultBody: Users log in about once a day, so the cache hits only 12% of logins. The other 88% still fan out to all 32 shards and shard CPU barely moves.

hints: The query does not include the shard key.
Making each of the 32 queries faster does not remove the 32.
Store a small mapping, partitioned by the field you do have, that points to the shard key.

incidents.title: Promo week pins a small Postgres at 99% CPU
incidents.brief: Tidepool's only Postgres runs on a 2-vCPU burstable instance. A five-day podcast promo tripled writes to 1,500/s; CPU credits ran out, so the node is throttled at 99% CPU and p95 is 2.4 s.
incidents.constraint: The whole database is 60 GB, traffic returns to normal next week, and the team is two engineers.
incidents.question: What gets Tidepool through the promo safely?

choices.label: Upsize to an 8-vCPU non-burstable instance for the promo

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Pay for a bigger box for a week instead of building shard routing for a load that goes away.

choices.resultTitle: Four times the cores, one minute of failover
choices.resultBody: A Multi-AZ resize fails over to the larger standby in about a minute. Sixty gigabytes and 1,500 writes/s fit one 8-vCPU node with room to spare, so CPU drops to 34% and p95 to 45 ms. Cost: about $400 more this month, reversible next week.

choices.label: Hash-shard customers across four Postgres nodes this week
choices.resultTitle: The promo ends before the migration
choices.resultBody: Two engineers spend the week adding shard routing and backfilling 60 GB while the throttled primary stays at 99% CPU. The promo is over before cutover, and the app now carries cross-shard queries for a load that fits one node.

choices.label: Move the orders table onto a separate shard with its own router
choices.resultTitle: Two small boxes, both out of credits
choices.resultBody: Orders move to a second burstable node, which runs out of credits within a day. Joins between orders and customers now cross the network, checkout p95 stays above 1.5 s, and the migration eats the promo week.

hints: Ask whether this load is permanent and whether the data outgrows one machine.
Burstable instances run fast only while they have CPU credits left.
Sixty gigabytes and 1,500 writes/s is well within a single mid-size node.
